evidence: Reads as: "Your future self probably also knows why you can’t pull this off perfectly today. What would they do for you, if they were here?" The old "That future you" was a demonstrative with nothing before it (C02); "Your future self" is a self-contained noun phrase that names what it means and does not need an antecedent. The previous paragraph still supports it: under the heading Borrow Hindsight it asks how "I" would respond "once I understood it more clearly", so a reader meets the idea of a later, wiser self in the same breath, and "also knows" lines up with that wiser understanding. The following "they" and the closing paragraph ("a wiser future version of whoever else is involved") both rest on a future self having been named, which this now does. The phrase is the author's own, used in line 29 ("Your future self might work"). Slight note, not blocking: this is the first appearance of the term in the section, so a reader gets it by inference from the heading and the previous paragraph, not by explicit introduction, but it is clear enough and "Your future self" is a plain, common phrase. No added claim, first person, bridge or announcement; no repetition issue ("future self" appears once in the section, "future version" once in the next paragraph, where it extends the idea).
